561.title: The call
561.hook: the leader calls the congregation to bless, and they answer; it needs a minyan
561.howItsDone: In a minyan, the prayer leader calls out Barchu before the Shema and its blessings in the morning and evening services, and before each Torah reading; the congregation answers aloud, and many bow.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yishtabach, the final chord of the verses of song. Your line was praised forever. Today, a new part of the service begins with a call.

Much of the morning service can be prayed alone at a kitchen table. The blessings for waking, the study, the psalms: they work with a congregation of one. A few moments don't. The Kaddish is one. And right after the half Kaddish that follows Yishtabach comes another. The prayer leader turns toward the room and calls out two words, and the room has to answer. With fewer than ten people there, the call isn't said at all. It's the hinge of the morning: before it, the verses of song; after it, the Shema and its blessings.
screen: `MUCH OF THE SERVICE WORKS ALONE.` → `A FEW MOMENTS DON'T.` → `THE HINGE OF THE MORNING.`

segments.voice: The leader says: Barchu et Adonai hamevorach. Bless the LORD, the blessed one. The congregation answers: Baruch Adonai hamevorach le'olam va'ed. Blessed is the LORD, the blessed one, forever and ever. Then the leader repeats the answer, so the one who called isn't left out of the response. Many people bow as they say it. It's the same call that opens a reading from the Torah. The idea of calling others to praise is old. A psalm says, in the old Jewish translation: "O magnify the LORD with me, and let us exalt His name together." With me. Together. Why ten? The Talmud, in tractate Berakhot, teaches that any matter of holiness needs at least ten people, a minyan. It learns the number by a chain of verses: the word congregation, used for the ten spies in the wilderness, links to the verse that says God will be hallowed among the children of Israel. So a congregation, for these purposes, starts at ten. Communities differ on who counts toward the ten: in Orthodox practice, ten adult men; in other communities, ten adults of any gender. All of them share the shape. One voice calls. Many answer. And the caller answers too, so nobody in the room is left out of the blessing.

segments.voice: Think of the voices that call to you in a day: the ones you answer fast, like an alarm or a boss, and the ones left hanging, like a friend who texted twice or a child asking you to come look. Pick one, picture the person on the other end, and picture yourself answering the way a room answers Barchu: all at once, and glad to.

562.title: Light, renewed daily (Isaiah 45:7)
562.hook: the first blessing praises God who forms light and renews creation every day
562.howItsDone: Yotzer Or is the first of the blessings before the Shema in the morning service, said right after Barchu; on Shabbat and festivals it is expanded with additional hymns.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Barchu, the call a whole room answers. Your line was answer the call. Today, the first blessing after the call.

There's a verse from Isaiah that the prayer book borrows, and then quietly changes by one word. That's unusual. The verse is God speaking through the prophet: I form the light and create darkness, I make peace and create evil. The rabbis wanted it for the first blessing before the morning Shema. But they didn't want the word evil in a morning blessing. So they swapped it.
screen: `A VERSE FROM ISAIAH.` → `ONE WORD CHANGED.` → `THE BLESSING THAT GREETS DAYLIGHT.`

segments.voice: In the old Jewish translation, Isaiah forty-five reads: "I form the light, and create darkness; I make peace, and create evil; I am the LORD, that doeth all these things." The morning blessing begins: blessed are you, yotzer or, who forms light and creates darkness, who makes peace and creates all things. Evil became all. The Talmud, in tractate Berakhot, notices the change and gives a reason: it's a more graceful way to say it. The meaning holds, because all includes everything, but the morning doesn't open with the word evil on your lips. The blessing over daylight mentions darkness, too, and the Talmud says that's deliberate: you mention night in the day, and day at night. Then comes the line behind today's carry. God, the blessing says, in his goodness renews every day, continually, the work of creation. Hamechadesh. Renews. Not created once, long ago, and left running like a clock. Made new, today. Some Hasidic teachers later pressed the idea further: if creation is renewed continually, it's renewed every moment, and nothing simply carries on by itself. Whatever you make of that, the blessing's picture is plain. Each sunrise isn't a rerun. It's the world being given again.

segments.voice: Find the nearest light, a window, a lamp, a patch of sun on the floor, and notice its color and the edges of the shadows it makes. Imagine it didn't exist a moment ago and has just been given, new, for you to see by. If you pray, you can say yotzer or, who forms light; if not, simply watch it.
Yotzer Or. Who forms light: the first blessing before the morning Shema, praising a creation renewed every day.
Your line: creation renewed daily. This morning's light is, in the prayer's words, new. That's day five hundred sixty-two.

563.title: Angels giving permission
563.hook: the blessing pictures angels granting each other permission before they praise
563.howItsDone: The angel scene inside Yotzer Or, sometimes called the Kedushah of the blessing, is said each morning before the Shema; it is often said seated, with people joining in aloud at holy, holy, holy and blessed be the glory.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yotzer Or, who forms light. Your line was creation renewed daily. Today, that same blessing suddenly fills with angels.

Two people in a meeting start talking at once, and both push on. Somebody else waits for a gap that never comes. Getting a group to speak with one voice is hard. In the middle of the first blessing before the Shema, the prayer book pulls back a curtain on heaven and shows a crowd doing it perfectly. Not because they're loud or fast. Because, before anyone says a word, they give each other permission.
screen: `TWO PEOPLE START AT ONCE.` → `ONE VOICE IS HARD.` → `A CROWD THAT DOES IT PERFECTLY.`

segments.voice: The scene borrows from the prophet Isaiah's vision. In the old Jewish translation: "And one called unto another, and said: Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of His glory." One called unto another. The prayer book reads that line closely and paints it out. The angels all take upon themselves the yoke of heaven's kingdom, one from another. And they give permission, reshut, one to another, to sanctify their Creator. Then they speak with a calm spirit, with clear speech, with a holy melody, all as one: holy, holy, holy. Where did the idea of permission come from? The old Aramaic translation of Isaiah, the Targum, renders one called unto another as they receive from one another. The prayer book builds on readings like that. So even angels don't simply start. Each one waits, offers the others room, and accepts the call from someone else. The holiness comes after the courtesy. Then a second group of angels answers with a line from Ezekiel: blessed be the glory of the LORD from its place. Some authorities allow this angel scene to be said even by someone praying alone, because it describes heaven's praise rather than making the congregation's own call. Its picture is a choir where nobody grabs the first note.
screen: `ONE CALLED UNTO ANOTHER.` · `RESHUT: PERMISSION, ONE TO ANOTHER.` · `CALM SPIRIT, CLEAR SPEECH.` · `THE HOLINESS COMES AFTER COURTESY.` · then, large: `THEY GIVE EACH OTHER LEAVE.`

segments.voice: Think of a conversation coming up, a meeting, a dinner, a call with someone you sometimes talk over, and picture the moment you'd usually jump in. Now picture pausing instead and asking, can I add something, or turning to the quiet person: what do you think? Calm spirit, clear speech.
Reshut. Permission, leave — the word for how angels, in Yotzer Or, give each other room before they call out holy, holy, holy.
Your line: they give each other leave. Even angels wait their turn. See you tomorrow.

564.title: With great love
564.hook: the second blessing: with great love you have loved us; help us understand
564.howItsDone: Ahavah Rabbah is the second blessing before the Shema in the Ashkenazi morning service, said just before the Shema itself; many Sephardi communities say Ahavat Olam, everlasting love, in its place.

segments.voice: Yesterday, reshut: the angels who give each other permission before they praise. Your line was they give each other leave. Today, the second blessing before the Shema.

Kids learn from people who love them. A child will sit still for a grandmother's story far longer than for a stranger's lecture. Students try harder for the coach who believes in them. Love comes first, and learning grows in it. Soon the morning service reaches the Shema, with its command: you shall love the LORD your God. But right before it comes a blessing that says, in effect: before you're asked to love, hear how much you're loved.
screen: `KIDS LEARN FROM PEOPLE WHO LOVE THEM.` → `LOVE FIRST, THEN LEARNING.` → `BEFORE YOU'RE ASKED TO LOVE.`

segments.voice: The blessing begins ahavah rabbah ahavtanu: with great love you have loved us. With great and overflowing compassion you have had compassion on us. Then it turns to learning. Our father, our king, for the sake of our ancestors who trusted you, and whom you taught the laws of life, teach us too. Then a chain of verbs: put it in our hearts to understand and to discern, to listen, to learn and to teach, to keep, to do and to fulfill. Eight steps, from first understanding all the way to living it. Light up our eyes with your Torah. Let our hearts hold on to your commandments. Unite our hearts to love and revere your name. It closes: blessed are you, who chooses his people Israel in love. Now the order. The very next thing said is the Shema, with its line from Deuteronomy, in the old Jewish translation: "And thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might." The command to love comes right after a blessing about being loved. The Talmud, in tractate Berakhot, records two opinions on how this blessing should open: with great love, or with everlasting love, and leaves both standing. Later custom kept both. In the Ashkenazi rite, great love opens the morning blessing and everlasting love the evening one; in many Sephardi communities, everlasting love is said at both.

If you pray, you can ask in the blessing's own words: put it in our hearts to understand.

565.title: Gathering the corners
565.hook: many gather the four fringes of the prayer shawl before the Shema
565.howItsDone: Those who wear a tallit at morning prayer often gather its four fringes at the words 'bring us in peace from the four corners of the earth' near the end of Ahavah Rabbah, hold them through the Shema, and kiss them at each mention of tzitzit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ahavah Rabbah, the blessing of great love. Your line was great love first. Today, a small gesture near the end of that same blessing.

If you've ever been in a synagogue on a weekday morning, you might have seen it without knowing what it was. Partway through the prayers, people wrapped in big striped shawls reach out, one corner at a time, and gather the long knotted fringes into one hand. Then they hold the bundle close, often against the heart, and keep holding it. It takes a few seconds, and it's timed to one phrase in the blessing.
screen: `A STRIPED SHAWL.` → `ONE CORNER AT A TIME.` → `FOUR FRINGES IN ONE HAND.`

segments.voice: The shawl is a tallit, a prayer shawl. What makes it a tallit isn't the stripes or the fabric. It's the fringes, tzitzit, tied on its four corners. The Torah commands them in two places. In Deuteronomy, in the old Jewish translation: "Thou shalt make thee twisted cords upon the four corners of thy covering, wherewith thou coverest thyself." Now, the gesture. Near the end of Ahavah Rabbah, the blessing asks God: bring us in peace from the four corners of the earth. The Hebrew word for corners is kanfot, the same word used for the corners of the garment. It can also mean wings. So at those words, many people gather the four fringes from the four corners into one hand. Scattered threads, brought together, while the prayer asks for a scattered people to be brought together, echoing the prophet Isaiah's picture of gathering the dispersed from the four corners of the earth. They hold the fringes through the Shema, and in its third paragraph, where the fringes are commanded, many kiss them each time the word tzitzit is said. Who wears one differs by community. In Orthodox practice it's men, in many Ashkenazi communities from marriage and in many Sephardi communities from boyhood. In many Conservative and Reform communities, women wear one too. The tallit is usually worn for morning prayer, by daylight. Wherever the gesture is done, its shape is simple: four corners, one hand.

Tallit. The prayer shawl, with fringes on its four corners, gathered into one hand before the Shema.

566.title: Hear, O Israel (Deuteronomy 6:4)
566.hook: the Shema is said with a hand over the eyes, attention on one thing
566.carry: like the four fringes in one hand
566.howItsDone: Jews say the Shema in the morning and evening services and at bedtime; for the first verse, many cover their eyes with the right hand and draw out the word echad, and the line is traditionally said at the end of life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the tallit, and the four fringes gathered into one hand. Your line was gather the corners. Today, holding those fringes, the Shema itself.

The Torah itself says when to say these words: when you lie down, and when you rise up. So they're said every morning and every night, and at bedtime too. The Talmud tells that Rabbi Akiva, dying, said them, and drew out the last word until his breath ran out. Six Hebrew words. And when the moment comes to say them in the service, something unusual happens. People don't look up, or at the book. Many raise a hand and cover their eyes, and for a few seconds the world goes dark.
screen: `MORNING, NIGHT AND BEDTIME.` → `SIX HEBREW WORDS.` → `A HAND OVER THE EYES.`

segments.voice: In the old Jewish translation, Deuteronomy six reads: "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one." In Hebrew: Shema Yisrael, Adonai Eloheinu, Adonai echad. The Hebrew has no word for is, so translators have put this verse into English in more than one way, but the heart of it is clear: one. Start with the first word. Shema means hear, but in Hebrew it stretches wider: to listen, to understand, to take to heart, even to obey. And it isn't addressed to God. It's addressed to Israel, to the people: a declaration, said to each other and to yourself. Now the hand. The Talmud, in tractate Berakhot, says that Rabbi Judah the Prince, reaching this verse, would pass his hand over his eyes. The custom of covering the eyes grows from that. Close off everything you can see, and attend to one thing. The same page praises those who draw out the last word, echad, one, long enough to mean it. And in a Torah scroll, two letters of this verse are written large: the last letter of shema, an ayin, and the last letter of echad, a dalet. Together they spell ed, witness. Commentators read that as a hint: whoever says this line stands as a witness. Hear, in this reading, means more than ears: the whole of the attention, gathered, like the four fringes in one hand.
screen: `SHEMA YISRAEL: HEAR, O ISRAEL.` · `HEAR, LISTEN, TAKE TO HEART.` · `A HAND OVER THE EYES.` · `AYIN AND DALET: WITNESS.` · then, large: `HEAR, O ISRAEL.`

segments.voice: Rest your right hand over your eyes and let the dark settle. If you're Jewish, or you'd like to, say the six words slowly, drawing out the last one: Shema Yisrael, Adonai Eloheinu, Adonai echad. If not, simply listen in the dark until there's just your breath.
Hear. Shema: listen, understand, take to heart. The first word of Judaism's central declaration.
Your line: like the four fringes in one hand. Hearing, here, takes your whole attention. That's day five hundred sixty-six.

segments.voice: Stand in a synagogue at the Shema and you'll hear six words said out loud, strong, sometimes sung. Then the room goes quiet. Lips are moving, but nobody's voice carries. A line is being said in a whisper. It's not in the Torah, and it isn't printed as part of the verse. And on one day a year, Yom Kippur, the whole room says it out loud.
screen: `SIX WORDS, OUT LOUD.` → `THEN A WHISPER.` → `ONCE A YEAR, ALOUD.`

segments.voice: The line is baruch shem kevod malchuto le'olam va'ed: blessed be the name of his glorious kingdom forever and ever. The Talmud, in tractate Pesachim, tells where it comes from. Jacob lies dying, his twelve sons around him. He's afraid one of them has drifted from his faith. The sons answer with the words of the Shema, using his other name, Israel: hear, O Israel, our father, the LORD is our God, the LORD is one. Just as there is only one in your heart, so in ours. And Jacob, relieved, answers: blessed be the name of his glorious kingdom forever and ever. So the rabbis faced a puzzle. Should we say Jacob's line? Moses didn't write it in the Torah. Should we leave it out? Jacob said it. Their answer: say it, quietly. They compare it to a king's daughter who craved a spiced dish; to say so openly would embarrass her, to go without would hurt her, so her servants brought it to her in secret. A midrash tells another story: Moses overheard the line from the angels and brought it down, so on most days people say it softly, as something borrowed. But on Yom Kippur, when people are said to be like angels, they say it aloud. It has a Temple history, too. On Yom Kippur, when the high priest spoke God's name, the crowd answered with this very line.
screen: `BLESSED BE THE NAME OF HIS KINGDOM.` · `JACOB'S DEATHBED ANSWER.` · `SAY IT, BUT QUIETLY.` · `ALOUD ONLY ON YOM KIPPUR.` · then, large: `SOME WORDS ARE WHISPERED.`

segments.voice: Think of something true you don't usually say out loud: thanks you're too shy to give, a fragile hope, love you haven't spoken. Breathe with it for a while, then whisper it, barely a breath, so only you can hear. If you pray, you can whisper the line itself: baruch shem kevod malchuto le'olam va'ed.
Baruch shem. Blessed be the name — the whispered line said right after the Shema, aloud only on Yom Kippur.
